questions.question: What is Euclidean distance measuring between two points?
options: The straight-line length of the displacement vector.
The number of coordinates in the larger point
The signed change in only the first coordinate.
The sum of the two position vectors
questions.explanation: Euclidean distance measures the straight-line length of the displacement vector $x-y$ between two points.
questions.source_support: Definition: $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$.

questions.question: Why do squared coordinate differences appear in the Euclidean distance formula?
options: They turn points into matrices
They give a length independent of sign.
They make negative distances possible
They remove all but the first coordinate.
questions.explanation: Squaring the coordinate differences combines the changes into a length that does not depend on their signs.
questions.source_support: Definition: $d(x,y)=\sqrt{(x_1-y_1)^2+\cdots+(x_n-y_n)^2}$.

questions.question: When is the Euclidean distance between two points equal to $0$?
options: Whenever the coordinate sums agree
Exactly when the two points are the same
Exactly when both points have positive coordinates
Whenever the points lie on a line
questions.explanation: $d(x,y)=0$ exactly when $x-y=\boldsymbol0$, i.e. the two points coincide.
questions.source_support: Definition: distance is the norm of the difference vector.

option_explanations: Equal coordinate sums do not force the points to coincide.

Lying on a line does not make the distance zero.

questions.question: Why is $d(x,y)$ the same as $d(y,x)$?

Because the square root changes sign when order changes
Because $x-y$ and $y-x$ have the same norm
Because $x-y=y-x$ for all points
questions.explanation: $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|=\|y-x\|=d(y,x)$, since $x-y$ and $y-x$ are negatives with the same norm.
